source_text: THESIS I. INter ea quae sunt in Scholis excogitata ad conciliandam libertatem humanam cum certitudine & immutabilitate decretorum divinorum circa actus humanos, increbuit in primis scientia illa conditionata, ex qua rationem istius conciliationis petendam esse censuerunt Ludovicus Molina & Fonseca Jesuitae primi, & post eos plurimi, tum in Schola Romana, tum inter ipsos Protestantes. Itaque, Deo favente, de concordia Libertatis humanae cum decretis divinis acturi, & varia Doctorum placita ea de re exposituri, ab illa scientia initium sumendum nobis esse merito duximus.
english: Of all the devices the schools have produced for reconciling human freedom with the certainty and unchangeableness of God's decrees about human acts, the one that has spread most widely is so-called conditional knowledge. The Jesuits Luis de Molina and Fonseca were the first to hold that the key to this reconciliation must be sought there. Very many have followed them since, both in the Roman school and among the Protestants themselves.

So, God willing, as we take up the agreement of human freedom with the divine decrees and set out the various views of the teachers on the question, we have thought it right to begin with this knowledge.

source_text: II. Igitur maxima pars Doctorum Scholae Romanae in ea est sententia, Deum non solum praescire ea quae libere & contingenter quidem, sed tamen simpliciter & absolute futura sunt; verum etiam illa quae, licet nunquam futura sint, libere tamen eventura essent, posita hac, aut illa conditione. Exempli causa, Deum non tantum cognoscere quid singuli facturi sumus ad finem usque vitae, in variis illis statibus in quibus, ex certa Dei Providentia sumus collocandi; sed praeterea quid facturi essemus, si plane diversus esset futurus rerum status, & aliae atque aliae agendi occasiones sese nobis offerrent.
english: Most of the teachers of the Roman school hold that God foreknows not only what will happen freely and contingently, yet simply and absolutely. He also foreknows what will never actually happen but would happen freely if this or that condition were in place.

For example, God knows not only what each of us will do right up to the end of life in the various states in which his sure providence is to place us. He also knows what we would do if the future state of things were entirely different and other opportunities for action kept presenting themselves to us.

source_text: III. Porro, cum praescientia eorum quae sunt absolute futura, necessario sequatur decretum aliquod divinae voluntatis, quo statuerit haec & illa agentia creare, & in hoc, vel illo rerum ordine constituere, atque cum illis, prout necesse est, ad agendum concurrere; hanc scientiam eorum quae simpliciter futura non sunt, sed ex hypothesi tantum futura essent, volunt in Deo praecedere liberum omne voluntatis decretum. Nempe juxta nostrum concipiendi modum, Deum, priusquam ullum de re quacunque decretum condiderit, certo & distincte novisse quid creatura quaelibet possibilis libere factura sit, si voluerit Deus illam creare, & concursum suum illi non denegare, atque haec & illa objecta, sub circumstantiis istis & illis ei proponere.
english: Foreknowledge of what will absolutely happen must follow some decree of God's will. By that decree he has resolved to create these or those agents, to place them in this or that order of things, and to concur with them in acting as needed.

By contrast, they hold that God's knowledge of things that will not simply happen, but would happen only on some supposition, comes before every free decree of his will. That is, to speak in our human way of conceiving, before God made any decree about anything at all, he knew with certainty and distinctness what any possible creature would freely do. He knew this on the supposition that he chose to create it, not to withhold his concurrence from it, and to set these or those objects before it in these or those circumstances.

source_text: IV. Quanquam autem ista scientia liberum quodvis decretum in Deo antecedat; nihilominus, ut patet ex dictis, in conditione sub qua res futura dicitur, includitur decretum, non quidem quod actu Deo inesse concipiatur, sed quod necessario in Deo ponendum esset ad hoc, ut res illa esse posset. Ac proinde conditionata illa futuritio, quae scientiae hujus objectum est, non desinit a quodam Dei decreto pendere: Verum non a decreto jam facto, sed quod faciendum a Deo supponitur, ut res illa vere futura dici possit. Nimirum more nostro Deus concipitur sic apud se cogitans, Si decernerem hunc Angelum, vel hominem creare, & concursum meum illi non subtrahere, in tali rerum dispositione hoc ageret, & non aliud; quanquam posset aliter agere.
english: This knowledge comes before any free decree in God. Even so, as is clear from what has been said, the condition under which something is said to be future includes a decree. It is not a decree conceived as actually present in God, but one that would necessarily have to be posited in God for that thing to be able to exist.

So the conditional futurity that is the object of this knowledge still depends on a decree of God. It does not depend on a decree already made, but on one supposed to be made by God, so that the thing can truly be called future. In our human way, God is imagined reasoning with himself: 'If I decreed to create this angel or this man and not to withdraw my concurrence from him, in such an arrangement of things he would do this and nothing else, though he could act otherwise.'

source_text: V. Id observat Gabriel Vasquez in primam partem Thomae, Nihilominus, inquit, dicendum est ita Deum certo cognoscere futura sub conditione, ut etiam sub conditione subintelligatur Dei decretum de concurrendo cum arbitrio, hoc modo, Deus bene novit, si Petro in hac occasione, vel illa, darem hanc, vel illam vocationem, & ego cum illa cooperarer, secundum quod illa postularet, nec miraculose subtraherem concursum meum, fieret tale opus: possem tamen subtrahere, si placeret: utrum autem Deus esset negaturus concursum, an concessurus, in eo casu nihil decrevit ipse. Tom. 1. disput. 67. cap. 4.
english: Gabriel Vasquez makes this point in his commentary on the first part of Thomas. 'Nevertheless,' he says, 'we must say that God knows future things under a condition with certainty in such a way that his decree to concur with the will is also understood within the condition. It runs like this. God knew well: "If on this or that occasion I gave Peter this or that call, and cooperated with it as it required, and did not miraculously withdraw my concurrence, such a deed would be done. Yet I could withdraw it if I pleased." But whether God would deny or grant his concurrence in that case, he himself decreed nothing.' Volume 1, disputation 67, chapter 4.

source_text: VI. Nec absimilia sunt quae leguntur apud Franciscum Suaresium. Adde praeterea, inquit, simpliciter totum hunc effectum pendere a voluntate Dei, ut absolute sit, vel non sit, & consequenter etiam in illis conditionatis debere in antecedente includi voluntatem divinam, scilicet, si ipsa velit talem effectum, vel saltem velit illum permittere, & ad illum concurrere; & hoc modo etiam illa scientia habet habitudinem ad voluntatem divinam sub praedicta conditione. Libro secundo de scientia quam habet Deus de futuris contingentibus sub conditione propositis, prius ratione quam de ipsa conditione aliquid decernat, capite sexto.
english: Much the same is found in Francisco Suárez. 'Add further,' he says, 'that this whole effect depends simply on God's will for whether it absolutely exists or not. So in these conditionals too the divine will must be included in the antecedent: that is, if God wills such an effect, or at least wills to permit it and to concur with it. In this way that knowledge also has a relation to the divine will under the stated condition.'
This is in book 2, chapter 6, of his work on the knowledge God has of future contingents proposed under a condition, before, in the order of reason, he decrees anything about the condition itself.

source_text: VII. Caeterum quemadmodum ad hoc, ut in tempore agant causae liberae, non putant necessarium esse, ut a Deo praemoveantur, & praedeterminentur ad hunc aut illum actum: ita quoque Dei decretum unde pendet sive absoluta, seu conditionata futuritio actuum liberorum, non putant esse decretum aliquod causas liberas praemovendi, & praedeterminandi; sed absque tali decreto, vel simpliciter posito, vel saltem supposito, Deum certo praenosse quicquid factura sunt agentia libera vel absolute, vel sub conditione. Nempe ad hoc, ut res fit & praevideatur futura, sufficere si ponamus, vel supponamus in Deo decretum de subministrando concursu, quem solum putant ad agendum necessarium, & qui talis est ex eorum mente, ut semper praesto sit liberis agentibus, nec illa ad agendum vel applicet, vel praedeterminet.
english: They do not think that free causes, in order to act in time, must be premoved and predetermined by God to this or that act. In the same way, they do not think the decree of God on which the futurity of free acts depends, whether absolute or conditional, is a decree to premove and predetermine free causes.

Rather, they hold that without any such decree, whether simply laid down or at least supposed, God foreknows with certainty whatever free agents will do, absolutely or under a condition. For a thing to exist and be foreseen as future, they say, it is enough that we posit or suppose in God a decree to supply concurrence. They hold that concurrence alone is necessary for acting. As they conceive it, it is always available to free agents and neither applies them to act nor predetermines them.

source_text: VIII. Porro hanc scientiam vocant scientiam Mediam, quoniam, juxta ipsos, medium tenet inter scientiam quae dicitur in Scholis scientia Visionis, & illam quae dicitur simplicis intelligentiae. Per scientiam autem visionis intelligunt notitiam illam qua Deus novit ea quae extra ipsum existunt in aliqua temporis differentia, nempe quae sunt praeterita, praesentia, vel futura. Quae omnia Deus ab aeterno tam clare, certo, & distincte cognoscit, ac si actu ipsi praesentia essent, non secus ac illa quae coram intuemur. Unde est quod dicitur scientia Visionis, ad similitudinem, scilicet, Visus corporei, quo res oculis objectas cernimus. Atque haec scientia dicitur quoque scientia libera, quia sequitur liberum decretum divinae voluntatis de rebus creandis atque conservandis, sine quo, ut nihil existere potest, ita quoque nihil potest videri praesens, vel praevideri futurum. Adeoque, si Deus nihil creare decrevisset, ejusmodi scientia Deo tribui non posset.
english: They call this knowledge 'middle knowledge' because, as they see it, it stands midway between what the schools call the knowledge of vision and the knowledge of simple intelligence.

By the knowledge of vision they mean the knowledge by which God knows things that exist outside himself at some point in time, whether past, present or future. God knows all these from eternity as clearly, certainly and distinctly as if they were actually present to him, just as we know things we see in front of us. That is why it is called the knowledge of vision, by comparison with bodily sight, by which we see things placed before our eyes.

This knowledge is also called free knowledge, because it follows the free decree of God's will to create and preserve things. Without that decree nothing can exist, and so nothing can be seen as present or foreseen as future. Had God decreed to create nothing, knowledge of this kind could not be ascribed to him.

source_text: IX. Per scientiam vero simplicis intelligentiae significant eam qua Deus novit & intelligit omnia possibilia rerumque essentias & connexiones omnes, seu necessarias, sive quomodocunque possibiles. Atque haec scientia dicitur naturalis, non libera; quia praecedit, juxta nostrum concipiendi modum, omne Dei decretum de rebus faciendis: neque potuit in Deo non esse, quanquam nihil extra se creare voluisset.
english: By the knowledge of simple intelligence they mean the knowledge by which God knows and understands everything possible, the essences of things, and all their connections, whether necessary or possible in any way at all.

This knowledge is called natural rather than free. In our way of conceiving, it comes before every decree of God about the things to be made. It could not have been absent from God even if he had willed to create nothing outside himself.

source_text: X. Scientia autem quam Deo tribuunt contingenter futurorum sub aliqua conditione, media ab illis vocatur, quoniam nec omnino convenit cum scientia visionis, nec etiam, cum scientia simplicis intelligentiae, sed de utraque aliquid participat. Nec enim est de rebus mere possibilibus, & abstracta ab omni consideratione existentiae, qualis est scientia simplicis intelligentiae: neque etiam est de rebus absolute futuris in aliqua temporis differentia, ex decreto Dei; qualis est scientia Visionis: Sed partim refert scientiam liberam, quia est de rebus libere futuris, si modo conditio poneretur, & in libertate Dei situm est, ut conditio illa ponatur: partim scientiam naturalem, quia praecedit omne decretum Dei, & Deus ea carere non potuit, etiamsi non decrevisset mundum, aut aliquid creare.
english: They call God's knowledge of things that would happen contingently under some condition 'middle' because it neither fully matches the knowledge of vision nor the knowledge of simple intelligence, but shares something of each.

It is not about merely possible things considered apart from any question of existence, as the knowledge of simple intelligence is. Nor is it about things that will absolutely happen at some point in time by God's decree, as the knowledge of vision is.

In part it resembles free knowledge, because it concerns things that would happen freely if only the condition were met, and whether the condition is met lies in God's freedom. In part it resembles natural knowledge, because it comes before every decree of God, and God could not have been without it even if he had not decreed the world or decreed to create anything.

source_text: XI. Nihilominus scientiam istam futurorum sub conditione nonnulli, non mediam, sed conditionatam simpliciter appellant, quoniam censent illam facile revocari posse, vel ad scientiam visionis, juxta quosdam; vel juxta plures alios, ad scientiam simplicis intelligentiae: quo de numero sunt Vasquez & Gregorius de Valentia. Quanquam observat Vasquez nihil obesse, si doctrinae & claritatis gratia, inter duas illas scientiae divinae species tertium aliquod membrum constituatur: atque hanc dissensionem vocum esse, non rerum, nec multum referre, si qui hac in re varie loquantur. Tom. 1. disp. 67. sub finem.
english: Some, however, call this knowledge of future things under a condition not 'middle' but simply 'conditional'. They think it can easily be reduced either to the knowledge of vision, as some hold, or, as many more hold, to the knowledge of simple intelligence. Vasquez and Gregory of Valentia are among these.

Vasquez does note, though, that nothing prevents setting up some third category between those two kinds of divine knowledge for the sake of teaching and clarity. The disagreement, he says, is about words, not things, and it matters little if people speak differently on the point. Volume 1, disputation 67, near the end.

source_text: XII. Caeterum scientiam talem Deo convenire, qua certo praenoscat contingenter futura sub aliqua conditione, probari posse putant Scripturae testimoniis, & argumentis ex ratione ductis. Et primo quidem ex Scriptura proferunt varia exempla praedictionum de iis quae non contigerunt quidem, sed quae, positis his aut illis rebus, eventura erant: Quale est illud quod legitur 1 Sam. 23. v. 11, 12. Ubi quum David rogasset Dominum, An si in Urbe Kebela maneret, Saul venturus esset ad capiendum ipsum. Et si ille venisset, An Kebilitae ipsum tradituri essent in manum Saulis? responsum accepit & Saulem venturum, & Kebilitas ipsum in manum Saulis tradituros, si in urbe Kebila maneret. Ac proinde utrumque istud, quod a libera Saulis & Kehilitarum voluntate pendebat, certo praescivit Deus, sub conditione quae locum non habuit, David fugam arripiente, qua de causa neutrum revera factum est.
english: They think it can be proved, both from the testimony of Scripture and from arguments of reason, that God has knowledge by which he foreknows with certainty things that would happen contingently under some condition.

From Scripture they first cite various examples of predictions about things that did not actually happen but would have happened had certain things been in place. One is 1 Samuel 23:11-12. David asked the Lord whether, if he stayed in the city of Keilah, Saul would come to capture him, and whether, if Saul came, the men of Keilah would hand him over to Saul. He was told both that Saul would come and that the men of Keilah would hand him over, if he stayed in Keilah.

So God foreknew with certainty both these things, which depended on the free will of Saul and of the men of Keilah, under a condition that never came about. David fled, and for that reason neither thing actually happened.

source_text: XIII. Simile est quod Deus interdicens Israelitis, ne filios, vel filias suas matrimonio jungerent cum filiabus vel filiis populorum a foedere Dei alienorum, hujus sui praecepti hanc rationem reddit, quod alioqui gentes illae exterae Israelitarum corda seducerent, & inclinarent ad Deos suos. Non ingrediemini ad eas, neque de illis ingredientur ad vestras: certissime enim avertent corda vestra ut sequamini Deos earum, 1 Reg. 11. 2. Unde patet, Deum certo praescivisse Israelitarum corda seductum iri, si illegitimis ejusmodi connubiis sese implicarent. Quod & in Salomone ob conditionem positam impletum est, in plerisque vero aliis Israelitis non item, propterea quod in illis locum non habuit illa conditio antecedens.
english: A similar case is God's command forbidding the Israelites to marry their sons or daughters to the daughters or sons of peoples outside God's covenant. God gives as the reason for this command that those foreign nations would otherwise lead the Israelites' hearts astray and turn them toward their gods: 'You shall not go in to them, nor they to you, for they will surely turn your hearts away to follow their gods' (1 Kings 11:2).

This shows that God foreknew with certainty that the Israelites' hearts would be led astray if they entangled themselves in unlawful marriages of this kind. It came true in Solomon, because the condition was met. It did not come true in most other Israelites, because in their case the prior condition did not occur.

source_text: XIV. Ex novo quoque Testamento multum urgent Christi verba quae habentur Matth. 11. 21. Vae tibi Corazaim, vae tibi Bethsaida: quia si in Tyro & Sidone factae essent virtutes quae factae sunt in vobis, olim sacco & cinere poenitentiam egissent. Ubi affirmat Christus poenitentiam acturos fuisse Tyrios & Sidonios, si eadem media Deus erga illos adhibuisset, quibus erga Judaeos usus est. Adeoque Deus, illorum poenitentiam sub ista conditione futuram fuisse ab aeterno noverat. Ac vim quoque faciunt in eo quod Dominus in quodam Pauli raptu jubet eum ocyus Hierosolymis exire, propterea quod non essent testimonium de ipso suscepturi. Nempe praevidebat Deus, quod si Christum Paulus Judaeis praedicaret, non essent fidem ejus testimonio habituri, Act. 22. 18.
english: From the New Testament they make much of Christ's words in Matthew 11:21: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.' Here Christ declares that the people of Tyre and Sidon would have repented if God had used the same means with them that he used with the Jews. So God had known from eternity that their repentance would have occurred under that condition.

They also lay weight on the passage where the Lord, in a trance of Paul's, tells him to leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people there would not accept his testimony about him. God foresaw that if Paul preached Christ to the Jews, they would not believe his testimony (Acts 22:18).

source_text: XV. Praeterea multis argumentis ex ratione ductis probari posse putant talem scientiam in Deo reperiri. Et primo quidem inde quod in propositionibus de futuro contingenti sub aliqua conditione determinata est veritas, vel falsitas, non minus quam in propositionibus de iis quae sunt absolute futura; ac proinde sunt illae quoque scientiae divinae objectum: quandoquidem nulla veritas latere potest intellectum infinitum, qualis divinus est. Propositiones autem de futuris contingentibus sub aliqua conditione determinate veras, vel falsas esse, ex eo conficitur quod inter eas vera potest esse contradictio, haud secus ac inter eas quae sunt de rebus absolute futuris. Siquidem prorsus haec sibi contradicunt, Si Petrus in talibus circumstantiis ponatur, peccabit, Et, Non si Petrus in talibus circumstantiis ponatur, peccabit. In omnibus autem contradictoriis, necesse est alteram partem contradictionis veram, alteram falsam esse.
english: They also think many arguments from reason prove that God has such knowledge. The first is this. Propositions about a future contingent under some condition have determinate truth or falsity, just as much as propositions about things that will absolutely happen. So they too are objects of God's knowledge, since no truth can be hidden from an infinite intellect, which the divine intellect is.

That propositions about future contingents under a condition are determinately true or false follows from the fact that there can be genuine contradiction between them, just as between propositions about things that will absolutely happen. These two plainly contradict each other: 'If Peter is placed in such circumstances, he will sin' and 'It is not the case that if Peter is placed in such circumstances, he will sin.' In every pair of contradictories one side must be true and the other false.

source_text: XVI. Deinde si verum est, quod Petrus positus in talibus circumstantiis peccet, sane non solum antequam in iis poneretur, sed etiam antequam in iis ex decreto Dei ponendus esset, verum erat, quod si in iis poneretur, peccaret, adeoque Deus ante suum decretum novit istud sub tali conditione futurum fuisse. Et prius ratione quam verum sit aliquid absolute futurum, verum est illud fuisse futurum conditionate.
english: Next, if it is true that Peter, placed in certain circumstances, sins, then it was certainly true that if he were placed in them he would sin. This was true not only before he was placed in them, but even before God decreed that he should be placed in them. So God knew, before his decree, that this would happen under such a condition.
And in the order of reason, before it is true that something will absolutely happen, it is true that it would happen conditionally.

source_text: XVII. Praeterea sapientis est priusquam aliquid decernat, animo conceptum habere quid secuturum sit ex rebus a se decernendis, atque faciendis. Cum ergo Deus sapientissime omnia decreverit, necesse ut ratione prius quam decreverit hunc, aut illum creare, taliaque illi objicere, & hoc, vel illo modo cum eo concurrere, nosset quid esset ex istis omnibus consecuturum, & quid, iis positis, creatura libere factura, vel omissura esset, qua in cognitione consistit scientia conditionata, de qua quaestio est.
english: Again, it is the mark of a wise person, before deciding anything, to form in his mind an idea of what will follow from the things he is to decide and do. Since God decreed all things with perfect wisdom, he must have known, prior in the order of reason to decreeing to create this or that creature, to set such things before it, and to concur with it in this or that way, what would follow from all of it.
He must have known what the creature would freely do or leave undone once all this was in place. That knowledge is precisely the conditional knowledge in question.

source_text: XVIII. Adde quod, nisi talem scientiam Deo tribuamus, infinitae poterunt quaestiones Deo proponi, ad modum illarum quas proposuit David, ad quas Deus nihil certum & perspicuum respondere poterit, nisi rem esse quae sciri non potest; quod non parum divinae omni scientiae detrahere videtur. Exempli gratia, quaerat aliquis, quid facturus fuisset iste, qui placida morte in Christo decessit, si oblatum ipsi fuisset martyrium? An si iste, vel ille talis puellae quae alteri nupsit, prior nuptias ambivisset, assensum fuisset impetraturus nec ne? si certus aliquis in regem Poloniae eligeretur, quomodo in illo regno sese gesturus esset? & infinita hujusmodi, de quibus cum homines sagaces, & rerum periti conjicere possint, non est verisimile ea simpliciter a Deo nesciri. Ac indignum Deo videtur, illum non certo compertum habere, quod homo probabili conjectura assequi potest. Quod si quis dicat, Deum talia quidem scire, & de iis distincte & perspicue respondere posse, sed talem scientiam praesupponere liberum decretum de rerum istarum futuritione, in hoc vel illo casu, inde sequetur in Deo esse infinita decreta de rebus nunquam revera futuris, ac proinde frustranea, inania, & otiosa quod valde absurdum est.
english: Besides, unless we ascribe such knowledge to God, countless questions could be put to him, like the ones David asked, to which God could give no certain and clear answer except that the matter cannot be known. That seems to take a good deal away from God's omniscience.

Suppose someone asks what a man who died peacefully in Christ would have done if martyrdom had been offered him. Or whether this or that man, had he sought the hand of a certain girl before the man she married, would have won her consent or not. Or how a certain person would conduct himself if he were elected king of Poland. There are endless questions of this kind.

Shrewd and experienced people can make guesses about such things, so it is unlikely that God is simply ignorant of them. It seems unworthy of God not to know for certain what a man can reach by probable conjecture.

Someone may say that God does know such things and can answer distinctly and clearly about them, but that such knowledge presupposes a free decree about whether those things would come about in this or that case. Then it will follow that there are in God countless decrees about things that will never actually happen. Those decrees would be pointless, empty and idle, which is quite absurd.

source_text: XIX. Veruntamen non pauci Doctores Scholae Romanae, & praesertim illi qui Thomistae recentiores dicuntur, praeter scientiam naturalem, quae dicitur scientia simplicis intelligentiae, & scientiam liberam, quae scientia visionis vocatur, negant in Deo dari scientiam ullam mediam, per quam scilicet, ante omne voluntatis suae decretum, Deus noverit ea quae nec simpliciter possibilia sunt, nec etiam sunt absolute futura, sed futura essent sub hac, vel illa conditione, & a creaturis intelligentibus hoc, vel illo dato libere fierent.
english: Yet a good number of teachers of the Roman school, especially those called the later Thomists, deny that God has any middle knowledge. Besides natural knowledge, called the knowledge of simple intelligence, and free knowledge, called the knowledge of vision, they admit no third kind.

They deny any knowledge by which God, before every decree of his will, would know things that are neither merely possible nor absolutely future, but that would happen under this or that condition, done freely by intelligent creatures given this or that.

source_text: XX. Putant enim nihil esse ullo modo futurum, vel absolute, vel sub conditione, nisi virtute alicujus decreti, quod actu in Deo praecedat, & quo Deus constituerit id quod futurum dicitur, vel efficere, vel saltem permittere; adeoque ante decretum divinae voluntatis praedeterminantis voluntatem ad alteram partem contradictionis, vel contrarietatis, non esse scibile quid in particulari faciet homo, vel quid facturus esset, si constitueretur in talibus circumstantiis; sed solum quid posset facere: idque quoniam ante tale decretum, res nec est futura, neque non futura, sed mere possibilis, & indifferens ad hoc, ut futura sit, vel non futura sit.
english: In their view, nothing becomes future, whether outright or on a condition, unless a decree actually comes first in God and gives it that status. Through such a decree God settles that what is called future will be brought about by him, or at the least allowed.

It follows that, until God's will has decreed to predetermine the human will toward one of two contradictory or contrary options, no one can know what a particular person will do. Nor can anyone know what he would do in such circumstances; all that can be known is what he is able to do. Before such a decree the thing is not yet future and not yet non-future. It is simply possible, and open either way.

source_text: XXI. Itaque non negant quidem quaedam contingenter & libere futura sub aliqua conditione a Deo certo praesciri, & in Scriptura praedici, quemadmodum Deus Davidi praedixit, quod si in urbe Kehila maneret Saul, venturus erat ad ipsum prehendendum; & rursus quod, si Saul ad urbem illam veniret, incolae erant ipsum in manus Saul tradituri: Sed pertendunt certam illam Dei praescientiam sequi liberum in Deo decretum, quo statuerit ut haec aut illa fiant, si adimpleatur haec vel illa conditio. Exempli causa, Deum praescivisse quod David manente in urbe Kehila, Saul venturus esset, & Kehilani essent Davidem tradituri, quia, posita illa conditione, Deus decreverat utrumque permittere, & ad substantiam illorum actuum voluntatem Saulis, & incolarum urbis Kehila praedeterminare. Prout latius videre est apud Didacum Alvarez de Auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 1. cap. 6. cujus Titulus est, Quod praeter scientiam mere naturalem, & mere liberam, nulla sit, etiam in Deo, scientia media constituenda. Et sequenti quoque capite, in quo Doctorum diversae sententiae objectiones dissolvit.
english: They do not deny that some things that would happen contingently and freely under a condition are foreknown by God with certainty and foretold in Scripture. God foretold to David that if he stayed in Keilah, Saul would come to seize him, and that if Saul came to that city, its inhabitants would hand David over to him.

But they insist that this certain foreknowledge of God follows a free decree in God, by which he determined that this or that should happen if this or that condition were fulfilled. Thus God foreknew that if David stayed in Keilah, Saul would come and the people of Keilah would hand David over. He foreknew it because, given that condition, he had decreed both to permit those acts and to predetermine to their substance the wills of Saul and of the inhabitants of Keilah.

This can be seen at greater length in Didacus Alvarez, On the Aids of Divine Grace, book 1, chapter 6, titled 'That besides merely natural and merely free knowledge, no middle knowledge is to be posited, even in God.' See also the next chapter, where he answers the objections of the teachers who hold the opposite view.

source_text: XXII. Quod spectat autem Protestantes, variae quoque sunt eorum hac de re sententiae. Et primo quidem illi qui in Belgio Remonstrantes vocantur, videntur communi consensu scientiam illam mediam qualis hactenus descripta est probare, & agnoscere Deum non solum quae sunt absolute futura praevidere, sed etiam quaecunque libere futura essent, in quocunque rerum ordine Deo placeret agentia libera collocare.
english: Protestant views on this matter also vary. First, those in the Netherlands called Remonstrants seem by common consent to approve of middle knowledge as described so far.
They acknowledge that God foresees not only what will absolutely happen, but also whatever would happen freely in any order of things in which God might choose to place free agents.

source_text: XXIII. Et primo quidem solennem a temporibus Molinae distinctionem triplicis in Deo scientiae, ut commodam refert Simon Episcopius. Observandum venit, inquit, triplicem Deo scientiam tribui solere. Unam, quae necessaria est, & practica, atq; simplicis intelligentiae dicitur, quae ex natura sua omni voluntatis liberae actu prior est, qua Deus seipsum & alia omnia possibilia intelligit. Alteram liberam, quae Visionis dicitur, & actu Voluntatis liberae posterior est, qua Deus omnia, quae facere, aut permittere decrevit eodem ordine novit quo ea decrevit facere, aut permittere ut fiant. Tertiam Mediam, qua Deus novit quid homines, aut Angeli pro sua libertate facturi essent, sub conditione, si cum his aut illis circumstantiis, in hoc vel in illo statu, aut ordine constituerentur. An haec divinae scientiae distinctio recte fiat, nos non expendimus. Quin ea commode & doctrinae gratia fieri possit, neutiquam dubitamus. Institutionum Theologicarum libro quarto, capite 19. De ordine & modo scientiae divinae.
english: First, Simon Episcopius reports with approval the threefold distinction of knowledge in God that has been standard since Molina. 'It should be noted,' he says, 'that a threefold knowledge is usually ascribed to God.

One is necessary and practical and is called the knowledge of simple intelligence. By its nature it comes before every act of the free will, and by it God understands himself and everything else that is possible.

The second is free and is called the knowledge of vision. It comes after the act of the free will, and by it God knows everything he has decreed to do or permit, in the same order in which he decreed to do it or permit it to happen.
The third is middle knowledge, by which God knows what men or angels would do in their freedom under a condition, if they were placed in these or those circumstances, in this or that state or order.

Whether this distinction of divine knowledge is correctly drawn we do not examine. That it can be drawn usefully and for the sake of teaching we do not doubt at all.' Theological Institutions, book 4, chapter 19, On the order and manner of divine knowledge.

source_text: XXIV. Nicolaus vero Grevinchovius prolixe pro hac scientia disputat in Responso quod opposuit Dissertationi de Redemptione generali, & Electione ex fide praevisa pag. 393. & seqq. Cujus Responsi examen instituit Guliel. Amesius in libro cui titulus est, Rescriptio Scholastica & brevis ad Nic. Grevinchovii Responsum. Et similiter Curcellaeus satis ostendit sibi probari scientiam illam Mediam seu conditionatam, quam in Scholis Deo tribuunt, dum in eo laudat Gomarum, quod ab Arminio edoctus, in posterioribus suis Thesibus, De Aeterno Dei decreto, & De Praedestinatione, Scientiam conditionatam in Deo agnovit; cujus ope, inquit, ingens illud ἄτοπον, quod Deum primi hominis peccati, & per consequens caeterorum omnium, quae ex eo fluere putantur, authorem faceret, a sua sententia amolitur. Praefatione praefixa libro cui titulus est Jacobi Arminii Examen Thesium Francisci Gomari de Praedestinatione.
english: Nicolaas Grevinchoven argues at length for this knowledge in the reply he wrote against the Dissertation on Universal Redemption and Election from Foreseen Faith, page 393 onward. William Ames examined that reply in his book titled A Brief Scholastic Rescript to Nicolaas Grevinchoven's Reply.

Courcelles likewise makes it plain that he approves of the middle or conditional knowledge that the schools ascribe to God. He praises Gomarus because, taught by Arminius, Gomarus acknowledged a conditional knowledge in God in his later theses On the Eternal Decree of God and On Predestination.

'With its help,' Courcelles says, 'he removes from his position that great absurdity which would make God the author of the first man's sin, and so of all the other sins thought to flow from it.' This is in the preface to the book titled James Arminius's Examination of the Theses of Francis Gomarus on Predestination.

source_text: XXV. Sed & inter Reformatos qui Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, reperiuntur nonnulli agnoscentes in Deo scientiam illam conditionatam, per quam ante omne voluntatis suae decretum, novit quid causa libera quaelibet, in quovis rerum ordine, pro ingenita sibi libertate, factura esset. Inter quos primum numerandus videtur Franciscus ille Gomarus, in hanc sententiam jam a Curcellaeo citatus. Etenim scribens in locum Matth. 11. v. 21. Postquam observavit Tyriorum Poenitentiam, posita miraculorum Christi conditione, futuram, intelligi hujusmodi, quae communis est Electis & Reprobis, credentibus & non credentibus: qualis, ex ejus mente, fuit Ninivitarum cum sacco Poenitentia; subjungit haec ipsa verba, Quod autem Christus de futura hac Tyriorum, posita illa conditione, poenitentia asserit, illius veritas ex indefinita divinae ipsius naturae praescientia constat, qua novit quidnam, quo posito antecedente, fuisset secuturum, etiamsi neutrum evenerit. Nam posita ea conditione, alterutrum fuisse eventurum, ut aut poenitentiam agerent, aut non agerent, omnibus notum est ex principio illo, quod duo opposita non possunt esse simul vera: sed utrum eorum fuisset futurum, cum res fuerit contingens, solus praevidit, qui infinita sua scientia omnia videt, nec solum necessaria, sed etiam futura contingentia certo praedicit. Similis locus est Ezech. 3. v. 6, 7. Ut refert Baldvinus Walaeus commentario suo in libros historicos Novi Testamenti ad locum Matthaei citatum.
english: Even among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some acknowledge in God this conditional knowledge, by which, before every decree of his will, he knows what any free cause would do in any order of things, according to its innate freedom. Francis Gomarus seems to come first among them, and Courcelles has already cited him for this view.

Commenting on Matthew 11:21, Gomarus first notes that the repentance of Tyre that would have followed Christ's miracles is to be understood as the kind common to elect and reprobate, believers and unbelievers. In his view the sackcloth repentance of the Ninevites was of this kind. He then adds these very words:

'What Christ asserts about this repentance of Tyre that would have followed under that condition is true by virtue of the unbounded foreknowledge of his divine nature. By it he knows what would have followed given an antecedent, even if neither came about. Given that condition, everyone knows that one or the other would have happened, that they would either repent or not, from the principle that two opposites cannot both be true at once. But which of them would have happened, since the matter was contingent, only he foresaw who sees all things by his infinite knowledge and foretells with certainty not only necessary things but future contingents too. A similar passage is Ezekiel 3:6-7.'
So Balduinus Walaeus reports in his commentary on the historical books of the New Testament, at the passage of Matthew cited.

source_text: XXVI. Robertus quoque Baronius expresse probat sententiam Fonsecae ponentis in Deo scientiam quandam conditionatam, ante liberum ipsius decretum, quae futurorum absolutam praescientiam antecedat. Deum, verbi causa, prius conditionate tantum scivisse quid eventurum esset, si Eva seducta a Serpente Adamum tentaret; postquam autem decrevit permittere ut Adamus obtemperaret uxori suae suadenti, non amplius conditionate, sed absolute praevidisse Adamum lapsurum.
english: Robert Baron also expressly approves Fonseca's view, which posits in God a certain conditional knowledge before his free decree, preceding his absolute foreknowledge of future things.

For example, God at first knew only conditionally what would happen if Eve, led astray by the serpent, tempted Adam. Once he decreed to permit Adam to obey his wife's persuasion, he foresaw no longer conditionally but absolutely that Adam would fall.

source_text: XXVII. Atque sic suam & Fonsecae mentem ea de re declarat. Nempe Quemadmodum illi qui sapienter magnum aliquod opus moliuntur, prius apud se cogitant quid ex eo consequuturum sit, quam absolute & determinate illud facere decernant; ita Deum Opt. Max. more nostro intelligendi, priusquam absoluta determinataque voluntate vellet mundum condere, quasi apud se deliberantem cogitavisse quid esset secuturum, si coelum & terram, & ea omnia quae in iis continentur, hoc ipso modo & ordine quo actu ea postea disposuit, constitueret, & scientia quadam hypothetica scivisse qui & qualis eventus evenirent, si res omnes eo modo & ordine disponerentur, quo jam dispositae sunt: neque Deum scivisse tantum quid eveniret, si causae naturales hoc ordine ac modo quo dispositae sunt, constituerentur: sed etiam quid eveniret si causae liberae haberent has occasiones agendi, aut non agendi oblatas, quas jam habent, aut quas causae liberae quae prius existebant habuerunt: Deum enim, cujus judicia incomprehensibilia sunt, certo cognovisse quid esset eventurum, si hae aut illae occasiones hominibus, vel Angelis offerrentur: exempli causa, Deum per scientiam hanc conditionatam novisse quid esset eventurum, si Adami uxor seducta a Serpente Adamo suaderet ut pomum ederet. In Metaphysica generali ad Theologiae usum accommodata sect. 12. disp. 2. num. 55, & 56. & pluribus aliis locis in eadem disputatione.
english: He states his own and Fonseca's view on the matter like this. 'Those who wisely undertake a great work first consider what will follow from it before they decide absolutely and definitely to do it. In the same way God, best and greatest, before he willed with an absolute and definite will to create the world, considered, as if deliberating with himself (to speak in our human way), what would follow if he set up heaven and earth and everything in them in the very manner and order in which he later actually arranged them.

By a kind of hypothetical knowledge he knew which events would come about, and of what kind, if all things were arranged in the manner and order in which they are now arranged. God knew not only what would happen if natural causes were set up in the order and manner in which they are arranged. He also knew what would happen if free causes were offered the opportunities to act or not act that they now have, or that free causes which existed earlier had.

For God, whose judgements are beyond understanding, knew with certainty what would happen if these or those opportunities were offered to men or angels. For example, by this conditional knowledge God knew what would happen if Adam's wife, led astray by the serpent, persuaded Adam to eat the apple.'
General Metaphysics adapted to the use of theology, section 12, disputation 2, numbers 55 and 56, and many other places in the same disputation.

source_text: XXVIII. Praesertim vero Antonius Walaeus in Academia Leydensi Professor agnoscit in Deo scientiam mediam, qua ex hypothesi res futurae cognoscuntur, etsi absolute futurae non sint, aut nondum sint. Et censet, verbi causa, Deum praescivisse Adamum sua libertate esse abusurum, si Deus eum talem conderet, donis ejusmodi ornaret, tentari permitteret, &c. & rem sic se habere de caeteris liberi arbitrii eventibus, ex Angelorum aut hominum arbitrio pendentibus. Atque hanc suam scientiam probat iis Scripturae locis quae supra citata sunt, & pluribus adhuc aliis, ut quod legitur Matthaei capite vigesimo quarto. Nisi abbreviati fuissent dies illi, non fieret salva ulla caro, Et si fieri posset seducerentur etiam electi, id est, nisi singulari gratia praeservarentur. Ex quibus & similibus locis manifestum esse dicit dari talem aliquam scientiam in Deo, ante omne decretum ejus, de eo quod certo futurum fuit. In locis communibus loco de scientia Dei, pag. 160. editionis in quarto.
english: Antonius Walaeus, professor at the University of Leiden, is especially notable. He acknowledges in God a middle knowledge by which future things are known on a hypothesis, even though they are not absolutely future, or not yet.

He holds, for example, that God foreknew that Adam would misuse his freedom if God made him such as he was, endowed him with such gifts, allowed him to be tempted, and so on. The same holds, he thinks, for the other outcomes of free choice that depend on the choice of angels or human beings.

He proves this knowledge from the passages of Scripture cited above and from many others, such as Matthew 24: 'Unless those days had been cut short, no flesh would be saved', and 'if it were possible, even the elect would be led astray', that is, unless they were preserved by special grace. From these and similar passages, he says, it is clear that God has some such knowledge, before any decree of his, of what was certainly going to happen. Loci communes, under the knowledge of God, page 160 of the quarto edition.

source_text: XXIX. Ibidem vero monet non esse necessarium, ut haec scientia hypothetica statuatur tertia aliqua species scientiae; quia illa ad scientiam simplicis intelligentiae pertinet. Nam illud, inquit, est absolute necessarium, ut Deus omnes modos possibiles causarum secundarum, sive solae, sive cum aliis agant, ab aeterno conspexerit, ac proinde quid ex unaquaque certa hypothesi posita infallibiliter fieret, vel non fieret, si causas illas produceret, eas conservaret, & cum eis hoc aut illo modo concurreret, vel hoc aut illo modo disponeret, aut disponi sineret. Hoc nemo Christianus negabit.
english: In the same place, however, he warns that this hypothetical knowledge need not be set up as a third kind of knowledge, since it belongs to the knowledge of simple intelligence.

'It is absolutely necessary,' he says, 'that God from eternity surveyed all the possible ways in which second causes act, alone or together with others. So he also surveyed what would infallibly happen or not happen given each particular hypothesis: if he produced those causes, preserved them, and concurred with them in this or that way, or arranged them in this or that way, or allowed them to be arranged. No Christian will deny this.'

source_text: XXX. Sed praecipue cavendum esse docet, nequis ista scientia abutatur vel ad decretum electionis a bono usu liberi Arbitrii hominis perpendendum, ut faciunt illi qui volunt, Deum priusquam hominem elegit, praevidisse quomodo, si haec aut illa gratia praeveniens & concomitans, in hoc aut illo ordine rerum, vel in hoc aut illo statu homini offerretur, ille per liberum arbitrium ei esset assensurus, aut non assensurus, adeo ut liberum arbitrium gratiam Dei eis determinet, non contra. Vel etiam ad negandam omnem Dei operationem efficacem in hominis convertendi voluntate, praeter moralem institutionem: quoniam, ut postea demonstraturum se confidit, Deus non tantum moraliter, sed etiam Physice agit in hominis voluntate, quando eum convertit.
english: But he teaches that we must take special care that no one misuses this knowledge. One misuse is to weigh the decree of election by the good use of a person's free choice. Those who do this hold that God, before electing someone, foresaw how that person would respond if this or that preventing and accompanying grace were offered him in this or that order of things or state. He foresaw whether the person would assent to it by free choice or not. On this view free choice determines God's grace for them, not the other way round.

The other misuse is to deny that God works efficaciously in the will of the person being converted, beyond moral instruction. As Walaeus expects to show later, God acts in a person's will not only morally but also physically when he converts him.

source_text: XXXI. Atque hanc scientiam futurorum conditionatam, & quae liberum decretum praecedat, in Deo admittit quoque Paulus Ferrius Verbi divini apud Metenses Minister Celeberrimus, Praescivit, inquit, Deus sua quam conditionatam vocant scientia, hominem quocunque illum modo faceret, hoc vel illud effecturum; ac proinde lapsurum si labilem crearet & tentari sineret, & ipsum sibi ipsi committeret, pro innata sua ipsius libertate ad utrumque, & creaturae infirmitate: si autem laberetur, futurum ut omnes perirent, si vellet, vel aliquos inde posset eruere, ut ita in illis justitiam, in istis gratiam suam declararet, &c. Et postea rationem divinae Providentiae circa lapsum hominis exponens, Primo, inquit, Deus praevidit fore ut homo caderet, si crearetur labilis & tentaretur. Deinde (quia vidit expedire ita esse) placuit ipsi ut hoc fieret, non inferendo vim homini, sed hominem ita creando, tentationique & sibi permittendo. Quibus subjungit, paucis interjectis, Deum circa lapsum Hominis nihil statuisse, quin prius praevideret, praesupposita libertate & tentatione, fore ut infallibiliter laberetur. In vindiciis pro Scholastico Orthodoxo, pag. 203, 209, & 210.
english: Paul Ferry, the celebrated minister of God's Word at Metz, also admits in God this conditional knowledge of future things, which comes before the free decree. 'By what they call his conditional knowledge,' he says, 'God foreknew that man would do this or that, in whatever way he made him. So he foreknew that man would fall if God created him able to fall, allowed him to be tempted, and left him to himself, given his innate freedom to go either way and the weakness of a creature.
If man fell, God foreknew that all would perish, if he so willed; or he could rescue some from it, so as to display his justice in the one group and his grace in the other,' and so on.

Later, setting out the reasoning of God's providence regarding the fall, he says: 'First, God foresaw that man would fall if he were created able to fall and were tempted. Next, because he saw that it was fitting, it pleased him that this should happen. He did not force man, but created him that way and left him to temptation and to himself.'

A little further on he adds that God determined nothing about man's fall without first foreseeing that, given freedom and temptation, man would infallibly fall. Vindiciae pro Scholastico Orthodoxo, pages 203, 209 and 210.

source_text: XXXII. Verum plures alii Reformatorum Theologi scientiam istam Mediam & conditionatam in Deo tanquam vanam & superfluam rejiciunt: non omnes tamen eodem modo, neque iisdem fundamentis nitentes. Et primo quidem nonnulli sunt qui concedunt omnes propositiones quae negant vel affirmant contingenter aliquid futurum, sub quacunque conditione, determinate veras vel falsas esse, ac proinde etiam a Deo cognoscibiles; nec enim ulli dubium est quin Deus omnem veritatem certo cognoscat atque apprehendat. Adeoque affirmant nullam esse quaestionem de futuris liberis & conditionatis, ab humano vel angelico intellectu imaginabilem, ad quam non perspicue respondere possit Deus, posita hac vel illa conditione, rem sic se habituram. Negant tamen inde sequi ullam esse in Deo scientiam conditionatam, quae liberum Dei decretum antecedat. Idque quoniam Deus ista quidem scit, sed ex libero voluntatis suae decreto, qua non tantum modos & connexiones rerum in tempore futurarum, sed etiam nunquam futurarum, & tantum fieri possibilium, apud se ab aeterno praefinivit; sed cum isto discrimine, quod ista fieri vellet, haec nollet: quae tamen si vellet, sic futura essent quemadmodum praefinierat. Quae sunt verba Matthaei Netheni apud Gisbertum Voetium, virum Celeberrimum, & eodem Voetio probante, Disputationum Theologicarum parte prima thesibus de conditionata sive Media in Deo scientia sectione tertia, num. 18.
english: Many other Reformed theologians, however, reject this middle and conditional knowledge in God as empty and superfluous. They do not all do so in the same way, though, or rely on the same grounds.

First, some grant that every proposition denying or affirming that something will happen contingently, under any condition, is determinately true or false, and so knowable by God. No one doubts that God knows and grasps every truth with certainty. So they affirm that no question about free and conditional future things that a human or angelic mind can imagine is one God cannot answer clearly: given this or that condition, the matter will turn out thus.

Yet they deny that it follows that God has any conditional knowledge preceding his free decree. God does know these things, but from the free decree of his will. By that decree he predefined with himself from eternity the modes and connections not only of things that will happen in time but also of things that never will and are merely possible. There is this difference: the former he willed to happen, the latter he did not. Yet if he had willed them, they would happen just as he had predefined.

These are the words of Matthias Nethenus, given in the work of the celebrated Gisbertus Voetius and approved by Voetius himself: Theological Disputations, part 1, theses on conditional or middle knowledge in God, section 3, number 18.
